# Generated Docs Checked by CI Diff

Generate documentation from the data, **commit the output**, and then have CI regenerate it and fail
the build if the result differs. The committed file stays readable on GitHub without running
anything; the diff check makes it impossible for it to go stale.

It is the one mechanism in the source set that structurally cannot drift, which is why it earns a
page next to [[documentation-drift]].

## The implementation

`build_docs.py` in [[labour-fraud-analysis]] emits four artefacts from `data/` — an ERD-and-columns
schema page, a per-column data dictionary, a coverage report, and a row-count manifest — under a rule
stated in its own docstring:

> "Run after anonymize.py so the numbers always match data/. No hard-coded counts."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/src/build_docs.py, 2026-07-11

`make docs` regenerates them. CI then runs the generator and compares:

> "git diff --exit-code docs/schema.md docs/data-dictionary.md docs/coverage.md data/_counts.json"
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/.github/workflows/ci.yml, 2026-07-11

The step is named "Derived docs are in sync with data/" — the assertion, not the action. Change the
dataset without regenerating, and the build goes red on that step with a diff showing exactly which
number moved. See [[github-actions]] and [[make]].

## Why commit the output at all

The obvious alternative — gitignore the generated docs and let each reader run the generator — is a
real choice, and [[python-programming-laboratories]] makes it, ignoring its build output as "all
reproducible from source". The case for committing here is that the docs are the **reading surface**
of a portfolio artefact: a reviewer opens `docs/schema.md` in a browser tab and never clones. The
diff gate is what buys the readability back without paying the staleness cost.

The same reasoning covers the committed SQLite database and the ported case file — see
[[generated-audit-artifact]] for the wider family, and [[reproducible-analysis]] for the seeding that
makes any of it deterministic.

## Where the gate ends — and where a claim outruns it

`confidence: high`, interview-confirmed 2026-07-28. This matters more than the pattern itself.

The README states that no value in the published dataset identifies a real party — "a claim that is
**test-verified in CI**". That overstates what CI enforces, and the workflow says so in its own
comment:

> "On a clean runner the private source + rules are absent, so the leak/stem scans skip and this
> enforces structural integrity + the PII regex sweep."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/.github/workflows/ci.yml, 2026-07-11

So the six CI steps split cleanly into two groups:

| Genuinely enforced on a clean runner | Cannot run there |
|---|---|
| lint; zero foreign-key violations; the four generated docs matching the data; PK/FK/row-count tests; the notebook executing; a regex PII sweep | the leak scan against a blocklist built from the private corpus; the stem guard from a git-ignored rules module |

The diff gate is real and it works. The privacy claim resting beside it is stronger than the
machinery behind it. Both facts belong on the page, and the honest version is the one the workflow
comment already tells: **a gate that depends on a private input enforces less in public than it does
on the author's machine, and the README should say which subset.** Recorded in full on
[[disclosure-gate]].

## The generalisation

Any artefact derived from data by a deterministic script is a candidate: schemas, API reference,
CLI help output, dependency inventories, fixture manifests. The requirements are only that the
generator be deterministic and that its output be small enough to review in a diff. Where those hold,
this replaces "remember to regenerate" with a build failure — and, as above, it is worth being
precise about which claims the gate actually covers.
